title: Why 10 to 20 mpg saves more than 25 to 50
description:
Miles per gallon hides how much fuel you actually burn. Flip it: over 10,000 miles, a 10 mpg truck burns 1,000 gallons and a 20 mpg one burns 500, a saving of 500. A 25 mpg car burns 400 gallons and a 50 mpg one 200: a saving of only 200, even though the car gained 25 mpg. Every step up in mpg saves less than the one before (50 to 100 would save just 100 more), which is why replacing the thirstiest vehicle wins, and why Europe measures fuel use in litres per 100 km. Duke researchers Richard Larrick and Jack Soll called this the MPG illusion (Science, 2008).

Numbers checked in code: every gallon figure, the litres per 100 km conversions, and 100,000 random pairs of doubled upgrades (the lower starting mpg always saved more). Sources: today.duke.edu/2008/06/gpmfuqua.html, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_economy_in_automobiles.

beats.say: Sounds backwards. The car gains 25, the truck only 10, and both double.
Your family has a truck and a car, and you can replace one. Each drives 10,000 miles a year.
Step 1: flip the number. Don't ask miles per gallon. Ask gallons for the year.
Step 2: the truck. At 10, it burns 1,000 gallons. At 20, just 500. You save 500.
Now the car, the one that gained 25.
Step 3: at 25, it burns 400 gallons. At 50, 200. You save only 200.
Step 4: push it to 100, and you'd save just 100 more.
Every step up saves less than the last, so fix the thirstiest one first. That's why Europe counts litres per 100 kilometres.
